title: Final: inside a type
sub: Objects on the heap, casts, primitives and dynamic
cards/0/q: An object on the heap of a 64-bit process. Which are true? Select all.
cards/0/options/0: The reference in a variable points at the word holding the type pointer (MethodTable)
cards/0/options/1: The object header sits 8 bytes before that word
cards/0/options/2: A boxed int takes 24 bytes on the heap
cards/0/options/3: A struct in a local variable also has a header and a type pointer
cards/0/options/4: GetType reads the type from the object header
cards/0/explain: A boxed int is an ordinary object: an 8-byte header, an 8-byte type pointer and 4 bytes of value, padded up to the 24-byte minimum. A struct outside a box has no overhead words. GetType reads the type pointer; the header holds bits for lock and the hash code.
cards/1/q: Equals compares fields, and GetHashCode returns 0 for every object. What happens to a dictionary that uses these objects as keys?
cards/1/options/0: Keys are found, but they all land in one bucket and lookups become linear
cards/1/options/1: The contract is broken: the dictionary starts losing keys
cards/1/options/3: Nothing changes: the hash only affects Equals
cards/1/explain: The contract demands one thing: equal objects produce equal hashes. Zero for everyone satisfies it. But there is a single bucket for all keys, and every lookup compares the key with each element via Equals — O(n) instead of O(1).
cards/1/wrong/1: A key gets lost when equal objects produce different hashes. Here the hashes are always equal.
cards/1/wrong/2: CS0659 warns that GetHashCode is not overridden at all. Here it is.
cards/2/explain: GetType is non-virtual and defined on object, so the int? is boxed first. A boxed int? that has a value is a box with a plain int. If x were null, boxing would produce null and the call would throw NullReferenceException.
cards/3/explain: The box holds an Int16. (short)o unboxes the exact type, then short widens to int implicitly. (int)o tries to unbox an Int32 from a box holding an Int16 — exception. An enum and its underlying type unbox into each other, and as returns null on failure.
cards/4/q: Match the IL instruction to the C# expression it comes from
cards/5/explain: Each 1 is boxed into its own box. == on two objects compares references, and the boxes are different. Equals is virtual: Int32.Equals runs and compares the values.
cards/6/q: A project with default settings. What does this code print?
cards/6/explain: checked only affects code written inside the block. The addition is in Add, and Add is compiled in the project context — unchecked, a plain add instruction with no check.
cards/6/wrong/1: checked does not extend into called methods: Add contains a plain add instruction.
cards/6/wrong/3: CS0220 is for constant expressions. A method call is not a constant.
cards/7/q: You want an exception instead of dropping the high bits, and then a type check plus unboxing in one step
cards/7/explain: checked turns the narrowing into conv.ovf, which throws OverflowException. The pattern is int i checks that the box holds exactly an Int32 and unboxes it. as does not work with int: on failure it has nothing to return.
cards/8/q: What is the compile-time type of n?
cards/8/options/3: It will not compile: dynamic has no Count
cards/8/explain: The result of an operation on dynamic is dynamic too: the compiler does not know what Count returns. So n.Foo() compiles and fails only at run time. To get compiler checks back, write the type explicitly: int n = d.Count.
